title: Look closer
hook: you'd travel to Olympia to see Phidias' statue, so why not look at the world's order? (Discourses 1.6)

segments.voice: Yesterday: it fits, the eye and the light made for each other. What fit did you notice that you'd usually walk past? Day three hundred ninety-six.

People fly across the world to stand in a crowd in front of a famous painting for ninety seconds. They wait in line, they get jostled, they hold their phones over strangers' heads. And then they go home and walk past the sky every evening without looking up. Nobody plans a trip to see their own street at dusk. Epictetus saw the same thing in his own century, with a statue instead of a painting. Today: look closer.
screen: `ACROSS THE WORLD FOR A PAINTING.` → `NINETY SECONDS IN A CROWD.` → `THE SKY, UNSEEN, EVERY EVENING.`

segments.voice: The statue was the Zeus at Olympia, carved by Phidias out of ivory and gold, so large the seated god nearly touched the temple roof. Ancient writers counted it among the wonders of the world. Epictetus says, still in Discourses book one, chapter six, that people travel to Olympia to see it, and think it a misfortune to die without having seen it. Then he lists what the trip costs them. The heat. The crowds pressing in. Nowhere decent to wash. Getting soaked when it rains. The noise and the shouting. And they put up with all of it, he says, because the sight is worth it. Then comes the turn. You don't have to travel at all to see the work he finds more marvelous: the world itself, and its order. It's here already. And you'd rather not look? Earlier in the same chapter he says something about why humans are here at all. Animals, he says, simply live. But a human was brought into the world to be a spectator of it, and more than a spectator, an interpreter: someone who looks and understands and says what they see. To finish your life without ever really looking, he says, is to miss the reason you came. That's the Stoic view, built on their belief in a reasoning God. But the practice in it needs no belief at all. The marvel you'd cross an ocean for may be on your windowsill.
screen: `PHIDIAS' ZEUS AT OLYMPIA.` · `HEAT, CROWDS, RAIN: WORTH IT.` · `THE WORLD IS ALREADY HERE.` · `A SPECTATOR AND AN INTERPRETER.` · then, large: `LOOK CLOSER.`

segments.voice: Choose one ordinary thing within reach: a leaf, your own palm, the grain of a table, the light on a wall. Look at it as if you'd traveled a long way and waited in a crowd to see it. Notice its color, its edges, how the light sits on it. When your mind wanders off, bring it back the way a tourist would, because you came all this way. Then breathe, and let the looking be enough. The bell holds the time.
Look closer. Epictetus' challenge: we'd suffer crowds and heat to see one statue, while the order of the world sits in front of us every day.
Your line: look closer. Today, give one ordinary wonder the attention you'd give a masterpiece: the sky, a face, a tree. Day three hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Readers of Epictetus often turn this chapter into a habit of deliberate looking: a minute each day spent with one ordinary thing as if it were a famous work of art.

myth: Epictetus says the trip to Olympia was comfortable
he lists the heat, the crowds, the bad washing and the rain.
he says humans came into the world to be spectators and interpreters of it
not just to live, but to look and to understand.
the Zeus at Olympia was made of ivory and gold
Phidias built the seated figure of ivory and gold.

fork.setup: you've survived the heat and the crowds at Olympia and seen the great statue. what does Epictetus ask you next?
options: why won't you look at the world's order, which is already here?
did it live up to the hype?
fork.reveal: he turns from the statue to the world itself: you'd travel for one, and you won't look at the other.

original.note: Greek theatēs: spectator, one who watches (our word theater shares the root); Epictetus says humans came into the world to be spectators and interpreters.

trapdoor: what you thought: travel to see the wonders.
what it means: the order of the world is a wonder you don't have to travel for.
what a scholar hears: Phidias' Zeus was counted among the seven wonders, so Epictetus picks the most famous sight of his age to make the contrast.

sources.ref: Discourses 1.6 (of providence: Olympia; spectator and interpreter)

notes: Discourses 1.6 paraphrased: the trip to Olympia to see Phidias' work, 'a misfortune to die without seeing it', the discomforts (heat, crowding, washing, rain, noise), humans as spectator (theatēs) and interpreter (exēgētēs). Confirm.
Phidias' Zeus: chryselephantine, seated, head near the roof (Strabo); one of the seven wonders. Confirm wording.
The opening tourist image (crowds at a famous painting) is modern and the script's own.
